The SeaTunnel Engine provides a command line tool for managing the jobs of the SeaTunnel Engine. You can use the command line tool to submit, stop, pause, resume, delete jobs, view job status and monitoring metrics, etc. You can obtain the help information of the command line tool through the following command: sh bin/seatunnel.sh -h The output is as follows: Usage: seatunnel.sh [options] Options: --async Run the job asynchronously. When the job is submitted, the client will exit (default: false). -can, --cancel, --cancel-job Cancel the job(s) by JobId. -f, --force-cancel, --force-cancel-job Force Cancel job(s) by JobId. --check Whether to check the config (default: false). --checkpoint-history Get checkpoint history by JobId. --checkpoint-history-limit Limit checkpoint history size (default: 20). --checkpoint-history-pipeline Filter checkpoint history by pipeline id. --checkpoint-history-status Filter checkpoint history by status: COMPLETED,FAILED,CANCELED. --checkpoint-overview Get checkpoint overview by JobId. -cj, --close, --close-job Close the client and the task will also be closed (default: true). -cn, --cluster The name of the cluster. -c, --config Config file. --decrypt Decrypt the config file. When both --decrypt and --encrypt are specified, only --encrypt will take effect (default: false). -d, --dry-run Validate or preview without running sinks. Supported modes: [static, connect, sample]. -m, --master, -e, --deploy-mode SeaTunnel job submit master, support [local, cluster] (default: cluster). --encrypt Encrypt the config file. When both --decrypt and --encrypt are specified, only --encrypt will take effect (default: false). --get_running_job_metrics Get metrics for running jobs (default: false). -h, --help Show the usage message. -j, --job-id Get the job status by JobId. -l, --list List the job status (default: false). --metrics Get the job metrics by JobId. -n, --name The SeaTunnel job name (default: SeaTunnel). -r, --restore, --restore-job Restore from the latest savepoint by jobId. --restore-with-checkpoint Restore from the latest completed checkpoint by jobId. -s, --savepoint, --savepoint-job Savepoint the job by jobId. --sample-limit Maximum rows forwarded from each source by sample dry-run mode (default: 10, max: 10000). --sample-print-data Print sampled row values to persistent logs (default: false). --set-job-id Set custom job id for job. -i, --variable Variable substitution, such as -i city=beijing, or -i date=20190318. We use ',' as a separator. When inside "", ',' are treated as normal characters instead of delimiters. (default: []).

sh bin/seatunnel.sh --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template Without --async, the client waits for the final job result. If a job keeps failing during task startup or automatic recovery, for example because a Paimon source lacks SELECT permission, the job returns FAILED after exhausting the configured retries and the client exits with a nonzero status. The --async parameter allows the job to run in the background. When the job is submitted, the client will exit. sh bin/seatunnel.sh --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template --async The -n or --name parameter can specify the name of the job. sh bin/seatunnel.sh --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template --async -n myjob

sh bin/seatunnel.sh --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template --dry-run static The --dry-run static (or --check) option validates the configuration file without submitting a job (for example HOCON/YAML syntax, plugin loadability, DAG topology, missing required options, and unknown connector keys). It does not run the full data pipeline. Plugin loading may read local JARs, so this is offline validation of the configuration file, not a strict zero-I/O sandbox. sh bin/seatunnel.sh --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template --dry-run connect The --dry-run connect option runs the static checks first, then uses connector dry-run hooks to infer source schemas, validate sink schema compatibility, and check connector connectivity. It may connect to external systems to validate credentials, permissions, and source or sink existence, but the framework does not create source/sink runtime instances, submit a job, read source records, create sink writers, execute save-mode logic, or write target data. Please note that dry-run validation is provided exclusively via the CLI. Connectivity validation is connector opt-in. Only connectors that implement the SupportSourceDryRunValidation / SupportSinkDryRunValidation interfaces are actually validated against their external systems. Currently supported connectors: Connector Source Sink Jdbc Yes (connectivity + schema inference) Yes (connectivity + table existence + field compatibility) Kafka Yes (topic metadata + runtime output schema, not consumer/group permissions) Yes (metadata + local serializer checks; dynamic topics have limited checks, Produce/transaction permissions are not checked) FakeSource Yes (schema inference only, no external system) - Clickhouse No Yes (initial-host connectivity + target metadata; no write permission or field compatibility check) MongoDB Yes (collection visibility + configured schema, MongoDB 4.0+, not document-read permissions) Yes (connectivity + configured authentication; no collection, schema, write permission or transaction checks) Neo4j Yes (driver connectivity + configured schema; not database/query validation) No RabbitMQ Yes (existing-queue metadata + configured schema; not consumer permissions) No S3File Yes (metadata connectivity + inline schema, single-table text/csv/json/xml; see supported scope) - Redis Yes (connectivity + authentication + configured schema; no key access) Yes (connectivity + authentication; no field compatibility or write permission check) Every plugin in the job is reported in a validation summary with one of two statuses: VALIDATED – the connector performed real connectivity and/or schema validation. SKIPPED – the connector does not support connect dry-run validation. A successful --dry-run connect result does NOT verify credentials or reachability for SKIPPED plugins. For sources without dry-run support, the schema fields declared in the config (schema / tableConfigs / table_list with fields or columns) are still used for downstream schema checks; if the config does not declare schema fields either, downstream transform/sink schema checks for that pipeline are also reported as SKIPPED instead of being validated against a placeholder schema.

sh bin/seatunnel.sh --master local --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template --dry-run sample --sample-limit 10 --sample-print-data The --dry-run sample mode has the following behavior: Runs the configured sources and transforms locally and prints their table paths and physical row schemas. Connector options and credentials are not included in schema output. Prints bounded source and transform row values only when --sample-print-data is set. Row values are hidden by default because persistent engine logs may expose sensitive data. Uses parallelism 1 for every action, including sources configured with higher parallelism, so the row limit is source-wide and the preview output is deterministic. Forwards at most 10 rows from each source into the sample pipeline by default, with a maximum --sample-limit of 10000. A source reader may finish its active poll or batch before it stops. Replaces configured sinks with an internal no-op sink, skips sink plugin creation and save-mode actions, and disables checkpoints. May read from external sources, but does not write to configured target systems. Supports local execution only. Cluster mode, asynchronous submission, restore, savepoint, validation, and job-control operations are rejected. Sample options are also rejected when sample mode is not selected.
sh bin/seatunnel.sh -l This command will output the list of all jobs in the current cluster (including completed historical jobs and running jobs).
sh bin/seatunnel.sh -j <jobId> This command will output the status information of the specified job.
sh bin/seatunnel.sh --get_running_job_metrics This command will output the monitoring information of running jobs.
documents.s: Getting The Monitoring Information Of Running Jobs

documents.t: The --metrics parameter can get the monitoring information of a specified job. sh bin/seatunnel.sh --metrics <jobId>
documents.s: Getting the Monitoring Information of a Specified Job

documents.t: sh bin/seatunnel.sh -s <jobId> This command will pause the specified job. Note that only jobs with checkpoints enabled support pausing jobs (real-time synchronization jobs have checkpoints enabled by default, and batch jobs do not have checkpoints enabled by default and need to configure checkpoint.interval in env to enable checkpoints). Pausing a job is in the smallest unit of split. That is, after pausing a job, it will wait for the currently running split to finish running and then pause. After the task is resumed, it will continue to run from the paused split.

sh bin/seatunnel.sh -r <jobId> -c $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template This command will resume the specified job. Note that only jobs with checkpoints enabled support resuming jobs (real-time synchronization jobs have checkpoints enabled by default, and batch jobs do not have checkpoints enabled by default and need to configure checkpoint.interval in env to enable checkpoints). Resuming a job requires the jobId and the configuration file of the job. Both failed jobs and jobs paused by seatunnel.sh -s <jobId> can be resumed by this command.

sh bin/seatunnel.sh -can <jobId1> [<jobId2> <jobId3> ...] This command will cancel the specified job. After canceling the job, the job will be stopped and its status will become CANCELED. Supports batch cancellation of jobs, and can cancel multiple jobs at one time. All breakpoint information of the canceled job will be deleted and cannot be resumed by seatunnel.sh -r <jobId>.

sh bin/seatunnel.sh -f <jobId1> [<jobId2> <jobId3> ...] This command forcefully cancels the specified job(s). After cancellation, the job will be stopped and its status will be set to CANCELED. This command supports batch operations and allows multiple jobs to be force-canceled at once. All breakpoint information of the canceled job will be deleted and cannot be resumed by seatunnel.sh -r <jobId>. Notes: If the job status is DOING_SAVEPOINT and the savepoint does not complete successfully, a forced stop (When the force option is enabled) will set the job status to CANCELED. A forced stop may leave checkpoint data incomplete or in an inconsistent state. It should be used only for exceptional or abnormal situations.

We can configure the JVM options for the SeaTunnel Engine client in the following ways: Add the JVM options to $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/jvm_client_options. Modify the JVM parameters in the $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/jvm_client_options file. Please note that the JVM parameters in this file will be applied to all jobs submitted using seatunnel.sh, including Local Mode and Cluster Mode. Add JVM options when submitting jobs. For example, sh bin/seatunnel.sh --config $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/v2.batch.config.template -DJvmOption="-Xms2G -Xmx2G"

SeaTunnel Engine provides server management commands for starting, stopping, and managing SeaTunnel Engine cluster nodes. sh bin/seatunnel-cluster.sh -h Server commands support the following parameters: Usage: seatunnel-cluster.sh [options] Options: -cn, --cluster The name of cluster. -d, --daemon The cluster daemon mode. -r, --role The cluster node role, support [master, worker, master_and_worker] (default: master_and_worker). -m, --member Show cluster members information. -h, --help Show the usage message.
You can get help information for server commands with the following command: # Start in foreground sh bin/seatunnel-cluster.sh # Start in daemon mode sh bin/seatunnel-cluster.sh -d

You can view cluster members information using the following command: sh bin/seatunnel-cluster.sh -m -cn my_cluster This command will output detailed information about all members in the cluster, including: Member ID: Unique identifier for each cluster member Address: IP address and port of the member Role: Member role (ACTIVE MASTER, MASTER, or WORKER) Version: Hazelcast version running on the member Example output: Member ID Address Role Version a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890 192.168.1.100:5801 ACTIVE MASTER 5.3.0 b2c3d4e5-f6g7-8901-bcde-f23456789012 192.168.1.101:5801 MASTER 5.3.0 c3d4e5f6-g7h8-9012-cdef-345678901234 192.168.1.102:5801 WORKER 5.3.0 Note: You must specify the cluster name with the -cn parameter. The cluster must be running for this command to work.

SeaTunnel provides a dedicated stop script to shut down cluster nodes: sh bin/stop-seatunnel-cluster.sh -h The stop command supports the following parameters: Usage: stop-seatunnel-cluster.sh [options] Options: -cn, --cluster The name of the cluster to shut down (default: seatunnel_default_cluster) -h, --help Show the usage message
# Stop the default cluster (seatunnel_default_cluster) sh bin/stop-seatunnel-cluster.sh
# Stop a cluster with specified name sh bin/stop-seatunnel-cluster.sh -cn my_cluster

Use these entry points first: Issue tracking: GitHub Issues Long-form discussion: dev mailing list Stable onboarding path: Contribution Path Contributor onboarding: Developer Setup and Contribute Plugin
documents.s: Where can I get help and join the community?

documents.t: SeaTunnel supports various data sources and destinations. You can find a detailed list on the following list: Supported data sources (Source): Source List Supported data destinations (Sink): Sink List
documents.s: What data sources and destinations does SeaTunnel support?

documents.t: SeaTunnel supports both batch and streaming processing modes. You can select the appropriate mode based on your specific business scenarios and needs. Batch processing is suitable for scheduled data integration tasks, while streaming processing is ideal for real-time integration and Change Data Capture (CDC).
documents.s: Does SeaTunnel support batch and streaming processing?

documents.t: Spark and Flink are not mandatory. SeaTunnel supports Zeta, Spark, and Flink as integration engines, allowing you to choose one based on your needs. The community highly recommends Zeta, a new generation high-performance integration engine specifically designed for integration scenarios. Zeta is affectionately called "Ultraman Zeta" by community users! The community offers extensive support for Zeta, making it the most feature-rich option.
documents.s: Is it necessary to install engines like Spark or Flink when using SeaTunnel?

documents.t: SeaTunnel supports multiple data transformation functions, including field mapping, data filtering, data format conversion, and more. You can implement data transformations through the transform module in the configuration file. For more details, refer to the SeaTunnel Transform Documentation.
documents.s: What data transformation functions does SeaTunnel provide?

documents.t: Yes, SeaTunnel supports custom data cleansing rules. You can configure custom rules in the transform module, such as cleaning up dirty data, removing invalid records, or converting fields.
documents.s: Can SeaTunnel support custom data cleansing rules?

documents.t: SeaTunnel supports incremental data integration. For example, the CDC connector allows real-time capture of data changes, which is ideal for scenarios requiring real-time data integration.
documents.s: Does SeaTunnel support real-time incremental integration?

documents.t: SeaTunnel currently supports MongoDB CDC, MySQL CDC, OpenGauss CDC, Oracle CDC, PostgreSQL CDC, SQL Server CDC, TiDB CDC, DB2 CDC, OceanBase CDC, Vitess CDC, and more. For more details, refer to the Source List.
documents.s: What CDC data sources are currently supported by SeaTunnel?

documents.t: Please refer to the official SeaTunnel documentation for the necessary steps to enable permissions for each connector’s CDC functionality.
documents.s: How do I enable permissions required for SeaTunnel CDC integration?

documents.t: Yes, SeaTunnel supports CDC from MySQL replicas by subscribing to binlog logs, which are then parsed on the SeaTunnel server.
documents.s: Does SeaTunnel support CDC from MySQL replicas? How are logs pulled?

documents.t: Yes, with limitations. Without a unique key the downstream sink cannot tell apart two identical rows, so updates and deletes may affect both of them. For a table without a primary key, the JDBC-based CDC connectors (MySQL, OpenGauss, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, DB2) fall back to a non-nullable unique-key column as the snapshot split column; when no suitable key column exists, the table is read as a single snapshot split. You can also point the splitter at a column explicitly with table-names-config.primaryKeys or snapshotSplitColumn. Two further limitations apply: parallel snapshot reading needs such a key column, and exactly_once = true requires a primary key or a non-nullable unique key, otherwise the job fails at startup.
documents.s: Does SeaTunnel support CDC integration for tables without primary keys?

documents.t: Before starting an integration task, you can select different handling schemes for existing table structures on the target side, controlled via the schema_save_mode parameter. Available options include: RECREATE_SCHEMA: Creates the table if it does not exist; if the table exists, it is deleted and recreated. CREATE_SCHEMA_WHEN_NOT_EXIST: Creates the table if it does not exist; skips creation if the table already exists. ERROR_WHEN_SCHEMA_NOT_EXIST: Throws an error if the table does not exist. IGNORE: Ignores table handling. Many connectors currently support automatic table creation. Refer to the specific connector documentation, such as Jdbc sink, for more information. For cross-sink behavior and the relationship with generate_sink_sql, see Sink Write Modes and Save Modes.
documents.s: Does SeaTunnel support automatic table creation?

documents.t: Yes, you can specify different processing schemes for existing data on the target side before starting an integration task, controlled via the data_save_mode parameter. Available options include: DROP_DATA: Retains the database structure but deletes the data. APPEND_DATA: Retains both the database structure and data. CUSTOM_PROCESSING: User-defined processing. ERROR_WHEN_DATA_EXISTS: Throws an error if data already exists. Many connectors support handling existing data; please refer to the respective connector documentation, such as Jdbc sink. Note: for JDBC sink, when sink query is configured (custom write SQL), save mode handling is currently not applied, so CUSTOM_PROCESSING/custom_sql will not be executed. For connector support boundaries and file/object-storage sink behavior, see Sink Write Modes and Save Modes.
documents.s: Does SeaTunnel support handling existing data before starting a data integration task?

documents.t: Use generate_sink_sql = true with database, table, and usually primary_keys when you want SeaTunnel to generate INSERT, UPSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements and apply save mode handling. Use query only when you must fully control the per-row SQL statement. Do not configure both modes. For the complete decision table, see Sink Write Modes and Save Modes.
documents.s: Should I use generate_sink_sql or query in JDBC Sink?

documents.t: SeaTunnel supports exactly-once consistency for some data sources, such as MySQL and PostgreSQL, ensuring data consistency during integration. Note that exactly-once consistency depends on the capabilities of the underlying database.

On some Java 8 hosts, the Oracle JDBC driver can block while obtaining secure random data for login authentication. If the operating system entropy supply is low, the client may not send the final authentication response before Oracle or an intermediate network device closes the connection. This is usually an environment problem rather than a SeaTunnel configuration error. For Zeta jobs, add the following option to the JVM that opens the Oracle connection: -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom For a job submitted with seatunnel.sh, start with $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/jvm_client_options; if the connection is opened by an engine process, also update the corresponding server JVM options. See Configure The JVM Options. Restoring the host entropy supply, for example with the operating system's rngd service, is also recommended. connection_check_timeout_sec does not control this login phase.
documents.s: Why does an Oracle JDBC job fail during login with Connection reset by peer and Authentication lapse?

documents.t: You can use Linux cron jobs to achieve periodic data integration, or leverage scheduling tools like Apache DolphinScheduler or Apache Airflow to manage complex scheduled tasks.

If you encounter issues with SeaTunnel, here are a few ways to get help: Search the Issue List or Mailing List to see if someone else has faced a similar issue. If you cannot find an answer, reach out to the community through these methods.
documents.s: I encountered an issue with SeaTunnel that I cannot resolve. What should I do?

documents.t: Would you like to declare a variable in SeaTunnel's configuration and dynamically replace it at runtime? This feature is commonly used in both scheduled and ad-hoc offline processing to replace time, date, or other variables. Here's an example: Define the variable in the configuration. For example, in an SQL transformation (the value in any "key = value" pair in the configuration file can be replaced with variables): ... transform { Sql { query = "select * from dual where city ='${city}' and dt = '${date}'" } } ... To start SeaTunnel in Zeta Local mode with variables: $SEATUNNEL_HOME/bin/seatunnel.sh \ -c $SEATUNNEL_HOME/config/your_app.conf \ -m local \ -i city=Singapore \ -i date=20231110 Use the -i or --variable parameter with key=value to specify the variable's value, where key matches the variable name in the configuration. For details, see: SeaTunnel Variable Configuration

If the text is long and needs to be wrapped, you can use triple quotes to indicate the beginning and end: var = """ Apache SeaTunnel is a next-generation high-performance, distributed, massive data integration tool. """
documents.s: How can I write multi-line text in the configuration file?

documents.t: Performing variable substitution in multi-line text can be tricky because variables cannot be enclosed within triple quotes: var = """ your string 1 """${your_var}""" your string 2""" For more details, see: lightbend/config#456.
documents.s: How do I perform variable substitution in multi-line text?

documents.t: SeaTunnel features a highly abstracted and well-structured architecture, making it an excellent choice for learning big data architecture. You can start by exploring and debugging the seatunnel-examples module: SeaTunnelEngineLocalExample.java. For more details, refer to the SeaTunnel Contribution Guide.
documents.s: Where should I start if I want to learn SeaTunnel source code?

documents.t: No, you only need to focus on the interfaces for source, sink, and transform. If you want to develop your own connector (Connector V2) for the SeaTunnel API, refer to the Connector Development Guide.
documents.s: Do I need to understand all of SeaTunnel’s source code if I want to develop my own source, sink, or transform?

documents.t: bin/seatunnel-application.sh is the only entry point of Application Mode. It exposes three operations, all of which target one external resource platform using matching deployment options, so status and cancel see exactly the application submit created.

bin/seatunnel-application.sh submit -t <target> [-a application.config] [-Dkey=value ...] [-c job.conf] bin/seatunnel-application.sh status -t <target> --id APPLICATION_ID -a application.config [--wait] \ [--wait-timeout <ms>] [--wait-interval <ms>] bin/seatunnel-application.sh cancel -t <target> --id APPLICATION_ID -a application.config The built-in help lists every option: bin/seatunnel-application.sh -h Usage: seatunnel-application.sh [options] submit | status | cancel Options: -a, --application-config Optional HOCON deployment file, e.g. application.config (not the job file) -c, --config SeaTunnel job configuration file (required for submit unless the provider supplies it, for example kubernetes.job-config-file) -h, --help Show the usage message --id Platform application ID (required for status/cancel) --job-id Optional native Zeta job ID for submit --restore-job-id Historical Zeta job ID whose latest checkpoint restores this new application * -t, --target External resource platform: kubernetes --wait Wait for completion (submit/status only; default: return immediately) (default: false) --wait-timeout Maximum time in milliseconds that --wait polls for a terminal status before failing with the last observed status; 0 waits indefinitely (default: 0) --wait-interval Status poll interval in milliseconds while --wait blocks (default: 500) -D Override a non-sensitive deployment option: -Dkey=value (syntax: -Dkey=value) (default: {})

Argument Operations Meaning submit / status / cancel all Operation, the first positional argument -t, --target all Resource platform that runs the application -c, --config submit SeaTunnel job configuration file; optional when the platform carries the job, such as a mounted job.conf -a, --application-config all Optional deployment file with common and platform options; options can also be supplied through -D -Dkey=value all Override one non-sensitive application.* or kubernetes.* deployment option, for example -Dapplication.worker-count=4; repeatable. Job ${...} variables are resolved inside the Pod, not on the submitting host --id status, cancel Platform application ID printed by submit --wait submit, status Poll until a terminal status --wait-timeout <ms> submit, status Maximum time in milliseconds that --wait polls before failing with the last observed status; 0 (the default) waits indefinitely. Requires --wait --wait-interval <ms> submit, status Status poll interval in milliseconds while --wait blocks; default 500. Requires --wait --job-id submit Native Zeta job ID to use for this application instead of a generated one --restore-job-id submit Job ID whose latest durable checkpoint restores the new application

Operation What it does Result submit Localizes the job, creates the application on the platform and starts it Prints the application ID and the native job ID status Reads the platform state and maps it to an ApplicationStatus Prints the application ID and status; a successful plain query exits 0; with --wait, follows the waiting exit codes cancel Removes the application and the resources it owns Prints the application ID and the cancellation result

submit returns as soon as the platform accepted the started application. Image pulls, admission and scheduling therefore never fail the command; add --wait to wait for the terminal status inside the same command: bin/seatunnel-application.sh submit -t <target> -a application.config --wait The job comes from -c or from a file the platform mounts inside the application, for example kubernetes.job-config-file. A submission that provides neither is rejected before the first resource is created. Values written as ${VAR} are resolved inside the running application, never on the submitting host, so platform-managed credentials can be injected through the environment. The deployment file (-a) is optional when -D supplies the required deployment options. When both are given, -D overrides file values. Platform validation still applies: omitting -a does not make incomplete deployment settings valid.

status reports one snapshot by default and polls that snapshot until it becomes terminal when --wait is given. --wait-timeout fails the wait with the last observed status when the limit is reached; the default 0 waits indefinitely, like an attached client. --wait-interval sets how often the status is polled. The platform-independent states are: Status Meaning CREATED The platform accepted the submission but has not started the control plane DEPLOYING The platform is provisioning the control plane RUNNING The application is running; workers or the job may still be starting SUCCEEDED The job completed successfully FAILED Startup, execution or reportable cleanup failed CANCELED The platform reported a cancellation UNKNOWN A known application has a platform state that cannot yet be mapped SUCCEEDED, FAILED and CANCELED are terminal; --wait stops there. It also stops at UNKNOWN when the platform cannot determine the application outcome. For both status --wait and submit --wait, FAILED exits with code 1, while UNKNOWN exits with code 2: the result is indeterminate, not a confirmed failure or success. SUCCEEDED and CANCELED still exit 0. A plain status prints the snapshot and exits 0, including for FAILED and UNKNOWN; query errors still exit non-zero. Do not interpret every non-zero exit as a failed application: if bin/seatunnel-application.sh status -t <target> --id "$APP_ID" -a application.config --wait; then result=0 else result=$? fi case "$result" in 0) echo "application status reported; inspect the printed status" ;; 2) echo "application $APP_ID outcome is unknown" ;; *) echo "application failed or the command could not complete (exit $result)" ;; esac

cancel asks the platform to remove the application. Every resource the application owns is deleted with it, while objects managed outside SeaTunnel are left untouched. How long a canceled or finished application stays queryable depends on the platform retention policy. Each platform guide documents the platform-specific behavior behind these operations.

Each submission creates resources with a unique application ID in the target namespace. The Job Pod runs the master. Worker Pods do not mount Kubernetes API tokens and communicate with the master through Hazelcast TCP.

The submitter validates the user-owned runtime ConfigMap, then creates a suspended Job with backoffLimit: 0. After receiving the Job UID, it creates the headless Service and, when kubernetes.secret.* or kubernetes.configmap.<entry>.data is configured, the owner-referenced application Secret and ConfigMap. After the API confirms the dependent resources, it unsuspends the Job and returns the Job name without waiting for the master Pod. A TCP startup probe gives the Zeta master its configured startup window; readiness and liveness probes then check the Hazelcast master port. Use status or Pod events to observe slow image pulls, admission or scheduling problems. The master starts an isolated Zeta cluster and creates a fixed number of worker Pods through the Kubernetes API. The master watches the application-labelled Pods through the Kubernetes watch API, so a deleted worker or a worker in a terminal phase is reported immediately; worker Pods carry no liveness probe. Workers join the master over TCP at its Pod IP and register slots; the headless Service only selects the master Pod. Pod phase is used for failure detection; Zeta registration remains the source of worker readiness and slot capacity. The master submits one Zeta job after every worker is ready. After the job terminates, the master removes workers and exits. The Job records Complete or Failed.

The submitter identity creates Jobs, Services, and the Secret/ConfigMap entries it declares, and performs status and cancellation operations. The application ServiceAccount only needs to read its Job and manage worker Pods. Only the master mounts the ServiceAccount token; workers do not access the Kubernetes API.

Hazelcast TCP must be allowed between master and workers. A NetworkPolicy must permit application Pods to reach the master port and required member traffic. The master does not provide task slots. Fixed capacity is: application.worker-count × application.worker.slots Pod requests equal limits. Namespace quota, LimitRange, admission policies, and node capacity can prevent scheduling. The Kubernetes API acknowledges Job, Secret, ConfigMap, and Service creation synchronously before the Job is started. Runtime watches are therefore used for externally changing Pod lifecycle state. A failed or ambiguous submission request compensates exactly the resources created by that submission, so pre-existing resources with the same name are never deleted.

The created Secret/ConfigMap and the Service are owned by the Job and are garbage-collected when it is deleted. Workers are explicitly cleaned by the application and carry application labels for fallback deletion. Referenced ConfigMaps are user-owned, shared by the master and workers, and retained after application cleanup. A caller-owned checkpoint PVC has no Job owner reference, so success, failure, cancellation, or TTL expiry does not delete it. Remote checkpoint storage is also independent of the application lifecycle.

bin/seatunnel-application.sh submits, inspects and cancels applications on Kubernetes. The shared command line reference defines the operations, arguments, wait semantics and exit codes; this page describes what they do against a cluster.

bin/seatunnel-application.sh submit --target kubernetes -a kubernetes.conf [-c job.conf] bin/seatunnel-application.sh status --target kubernetes --id APPLICATION_ID -a kubernetes.conf [--wait] bin/seatunnel-application.sh cancel --target kubernetes --id APPLICATION_ID -a kubernetes.conf

submit creates the owner batch/v1 Job, the Secret/ConfigMap/Service the application owns, and starts the Job: Application ID: example-9f2c41a0b7d3 Job ID: 917381145928572929 The application ID is generated from application.name, so it is also the Kubernetes Job name and the value of the ownership label on every owned resource. -c is optional when the deployment file selects a mounted job file through kubernetes.job-config-file. The command returns as soon as the API accepted the started Job, so image pull, admission and scheduling never fail the submission. When resource creation itself fails, the resources created by that attempt are rolled back before the error is reported.

status maps the Job and Pod state to the platform-neutral status: Application ID: example-9f2c41a0b7d3 Status: RUNNING A plain status prints the snapshot and exits 0 when the query succeeds, including for FAILED and UNKNOWN; query errors exit non-zero. --wait keeps polling until a terminal status or UNKNOWN is reported. Both status --wait and submit --wait exit 1 for FAILED, 2 for UNKNOWN (an indeterminate outcome, not a confirmed success or failure), and 0 for SUCCEEDED or CANCELED. See Status and waiting for the shared exit-code contract. --wait-timeout bounds that polling and fails with the last observed status when the limit is reached, while the default 0 keeps waiting indefinitely; --wait-interval sets the poll interval (500 ms by default).

cancel deletes the owner Job of the application. Owned Pods, Services, Secrets and ConfigMaps are garbage-collected through the owner reference; referenced objects created outside SeaTunnel are never modified or deleted. The command reports Cancellation requested once the delete is accepted. Because the owner Job is removed, a later status returns UNKNOWN; use kubectl to confirm that the Pods are gone. If the delete call fails before the Job is removed, retry cancel after the API outage is resolved.

Every platform resource carries the application ID as its ownership label, so the application can be examined directly: kubectl -n seatunnel-apps get jobs,pods,services -l seatunnel.apache.org/application-id=example-9f2c41a0b7d3 kubectl -n seatunnel-apps describe job example-9f2c41a0b7d3 kubectl -n seatunnel-apps logs job/example-9f2c41a0b7d3 tip Use status --wait for programmatic completion and kubectl for diagnosis; the command itself does not replace Pod events and logs when a start-up problem has to be explained. See Configuration for the deployment options these commands accept.
Recovery creates a new Kubernetes Job and a new Zeta job ID. This release does not provide automatic master failover or Job restart.

Supported choices include: a caller-owned PVC mounted at /opt/seatunnel/checkpoints in the master; HDFS; object stores supported by native checkpoint storage, including OSS, S3, and COS. note Remote storage does not require kubernetes.checkpoint-pvc. The image must contain the corresponding filesystem implementation and dependencies.

Create a claim: apiVersion: v1 kind: PersistentVolumeClaim metadata: name: seatunnel-checkpoints namespace: seatunnel-apps spec: accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce] resources: requests: storage: 10Gi Add the deployment option: kubernetes.checkpoint-pvc = "seatunnel-checkpoints" Configure native storage in the seatunnel.yaml stored in the runtime ConfigMap: seatunnel: engine: checkpoint: interval: 5000 timeout: 60000 storage: type: hdfs max-retained: 3 plugin-config: storage.type: hdfs fs.defaultFS: file:/// namespace: /opt/seatunnel/checkpoints/orders/ caution The provider only mounts the PVC. Native checkpoint storage interprets the backend and namespace. The master user must be able to write to the volume. The application never deletes this PVC.

Configure the complete seatunnel.engine.checkpoint.storage.plugin-config in the runtime ConfigMap's seatunnel.yaml. Application Mode does not parse checkpoint URIs or maintain a backend allowlist. See Checkpoint Storage for HDFS, OSS, S3, COS, endpoint, and authentication settings.

Enable periodic checkpoints and retain the Zeta job ID printed during the original submission: env { job.mode = "STREAMING" checkpoint.interval = 5000 checkpoint.retain-after-job-cancelled = true } After the original application has stopped and a completed checkpoint exists: bin/seatunnel-application.sh submit --target kubernetes \ --config job.conf --application-config kubernetes.conf \ --restore-job-id PREVIOUS_JOB_ID caution The new submission uses a new job ID and loads the historical job's latest eligible checkpoint. A missing checkpoint fails the job on the master (the submit command has already returned) instead of silently starting over. Keep topology, connector versions, state format, and parallelism compatible. Replay after the checkpoint and sink delivery guarantees depend on connector semantics.

Application Mode reads the deployment file (-a) with application.* and kubernetes.* options on the submitting host. The job itself comes from -c or from a file the platform mounts inside the application, for example through kubernetes.job-config-file. This page is the reference for the deployment file; see Quick start for the first submission and Checkpoint recovery for restore behaviour.

Source Configures Notes Deployment file (-a) application.* and kubernetes.* Resolved on the submitting host. Put sensitive values here, not on the command line. Option overrides (-Dkey=value) Any deployment option Resolved on the submitter too; command-line arguments may be visible to other users. Job file (-c) The job itself Optional: kubernetes.job-config-file can mount the job inside the application instead. Carried to the master verbatim, including unresolved ${VAR} placeholders, unless a mounted file is configured — then only the file is used. Pod environment ${VAR} values in the job Built from kubernetes.env, kubernetes.env-from.* and mounted Secret/ConfigMap files on the master. caution Command-line overrides (-Dkey=value) may be visible to other users on the submitting host. Keep kubernetes.kubeconfig and other sensitive values in a permission-restricted deployment file.

Name Type Required Default value Description application.name string no seatunnel Readable prefix of the unique Job name. application.job-id long no Generated Positive native Zeta job ID. application.restore-job-id long no - Historical job ID whose latest eligible checkpoint initializes this execution. application.worker-count int no 1 Fixed number of worker Pods. application.worker.memory-mb int no 1024 Worker memory request and limit in MiB. application.worker.cpu-cores int no 1 Worker CPU request and limit. application.worker.slots int no 2 Fixed execution slots per worker. application.master.memory-mb int no 1024 Master memory request and limit in MiB. application.master.cpu-cores int no 1 Master CPU request and limit. application.master.port int no 5801 Master Hazelcast TCP port. application.startup-timeout-millis long no 120000 Applied to worker creation and registration on the master and to client connection setup; submission does not wait for master startup. note Pod JVM heap uses 75% of the memory limit, leaving the remainder for off-heap allocations and JVM overhead. note application.startup-timeout-millis is not a job execution limit and does not bound submission. The submitter returns as soon as the API accepts the started Job, so slow image pulls, admission, or scheduling problems never fail the submit command; observe them with status and Pod events. The master uses the same timeout separately for workers.

Use kubernetes.image-pull-secrets for existing private-registry Secrets. note The provider does not create those credentials or expose an arbitrary Pod template. Local files and plugin JARs referenced by a job are not downloaded dynamically and must already be present in the image.

Two identities access the Kubernetes API. The master Pod runs with kubernetes.service-account and needs: Resource Verbs Required when Pods create, list, watch, delete, deletecollection always; create/delete/deletecollection manage worker Pods, watch reports a lost worker Jobs get always; reads the owner Job The submitting identity runs bin/seatunnel-application.sh and needs: Resource Verbs Required when Jobs create, get, patch, delete always; patch unsuspends the Job after creation Pods list, deletecollection always; list resolves the application status, deletecollection removes the Pods on cancel Services create, delete always; the headless Service that selects the master Pod ConfigMaps get kubernetes.configmap.<entry>.ref; without it the validation is skipped with a warning ConfigMaps create, delete only with a created entry (kubernetes.configmap.<entry>.data) Secrets create, delete only with kubernetes.secret Secrets get only with kubernetes.secret-ref; without it the validation is skipped with a warning The quick start grants only the verbs its demo job uses; add the ConfigMap get rule and the Secret rules when the deployment needs references or Secrets, then replace the submitter RoleBinding subject with your user, group or CI ServiceAccount.

Use kubernetes.master.node-selector / kubernetes.worker.node-selector to target a node pool, and the matching kubernetes.*.tolerations to tolerate its taints. Workers are created by the master at runtime, so worker tolerations travel inside the localized specification: kubernetes { master.node-selector = "pool:seatunnel" worker.node-selector = "pool:seatunnel" master.tolerations = "dedicated=seatunnel:NoSchedule" worker.tolerations = "dedicated=seatunnel:NoSchedule;spot:NoExecute" } Entries are key[=value][:Effect] separated by ;: a key without a value uses the Exists operator, and an explicit effect must be NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule or NoExecute. Without tolerations, the Pods stay Pending on a tainted node pool and report had untolerated taint events.

-c job.conf is read verbatim on the submitting host and carried inside the localized specification; the submitter only parse-checks it with placeholders left unresolved. The job may also come from a file inside the Pod, which is what kubernetes.job-config-file selects. That option is what makes -c optional: a submission that provides neither source is rejected before the first resource is created. caution The inline job text is carried Base64-encoded in the Pod template of the application Job, so anyone who can read Jobs or Pods in the namespace can read it, including credentials written in the job file, for as long as the Job is retained (kubernetes.finished-job-retention-seconds, 24 hours by default). Base64 is not encryption. Keep credentials out of the inline job, mount the job file from a Secret through kubernetes.job-config-file, or encrypt the affected values with config encryption, which the master decrypts at runtime. The option resolves to a file name under <seatunnel-home>/config or to the absolute path a Secret or ConfigMap key is mounted at. Before the job is parsed: Option unset (the default): the submitted -c file is used, so -c is required. Option set and the file exists: the mounted file replaces the submitted content, and the inline -c text is not carried in the Job object. Option set and the file is missing: the master fails instead of starting without a job; only a specification written by an older submitter still falls back to its inline text. The surviving text is parsed exactly once on the master, where ${VAR} is resolved against the Pod environment, so the submitting host never bakes its own values into the job. ConfigMap (recommended). Point kubernetes.job-config-file at a relative name and mount that key under <seatunnel-home>/config; no Secret permission is involved: kubernetes { job-config-file = job.conf configmap.job-conf { ref = platform-job-config mount.job.conf = /opt/seatunnel/config/job.conf } } Secret. Keep the Secret mount and select the mounted file explicitly: kubernetes { secret-ref = platform-job-secrets job-config-file = /etc/seatunnel-secrets/application/job.conf } tip Values written directly into the deployment file are resolved on the submitting host, but ${VAR} inside a quoted (or triple-quoted) value is carried literally, which lets created Secret or ConfigMap data hold a job file with master-side placeholders.

An application Secret has two mutually exclusive modes. Both mount the Secret read-only at kubernetes.secret-directory (default /etc/seatunnel-secrets/application) in the master and worker Pods. Point kubernetes.job-config-file at <secret-directory>/job.conf when the Secret carries the job configuration. Mode Configuration Lifecycle Reference kubernetes.secret-ref Created and managed by your platform; SeaTunnel never creates or deletes it. Create kubernetes.secret.name / kubernetes.secret.data.* Created and owned by SeaTunnel; carries the Job owner reference and is removed with the application. Reference an existing Secret. SeaTunnel only mounts it. Inject its keys as Pod environment variables when the job configuration uses ${VAR} placeholders: kubernetes { secret-ref = platform-job-secrets env.MYSQL_PASSWORD = "secret:platform-job-secrets/password" } Let SeaTunnel create the Secret. data entries are resolved on the submitting host and written into an Opaque Secret, whose default name is the application ID and can be overridden with name. Inject the created keys through kubernetes.env: kubernetes { secret { name = seatunnel-job-secrets data.MYSQL_PASSWORD = ${MYSQL_PASSWORD} # resolved on the submitting host data.S3_SECRET_KEY = "s3-secret-key" } env { MYSQL_PASSWORD = "secret:seatunnel-job-secrets/MYSQL_PASSWORD" S3_SECRET_KEY = "secret:seatunnel-job-secrets/S3_SECRET_KEY" } } A created Secret can also carry the job file; select it explicitly because the default path points at <seatunnel-home>/config: kubernetes { secret { name = seatunnel-job-secrets data.job.conf = """ env { job.mode = "BATCH" parallelism = 2 } source { FakeSource { row.num = 10 schema { fields { id = int } } } } sink { Console {} } """ } secret-directory = /etc/seatunnel-secrets/application job-config-file = /etc/seatunnel-secrets/application/job.conf } caution Keep connector credentials out of ConfigMaps: they are not confidential. Use a Secret with kubernetes.env/${VAR} when the job needs them.

Every kubernetes.configmap.<entry> entry mounts one or more files through subPath in both the master and worker Pods. Each mounted key must declare its full container path in mount, so SeaTunnel never assumes a configuration directory. Mode Configuration Lifecycle Reference ref + mount Created and managed by your platform; SeaTunnel only mounts it and validates the referenced keys before submission. Create name (optional) + data + mount Created and owned by SeaTunnel as name or <application-id>-<entry>; carries the Job owner reference and is removed with the application. Mount files from existing ConfigMaps. Use one entry per ConfigMap to mount files from different ConfigMaps at different paths: kubernetes.configmap { engine-config { ref = platform-engine-config mount.seatunnel.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/seatunnel.yaml } logging-config { ref = platform-logging-config mount.log4j2_client.properties = /opt/seatunnel/config/log4j2_client.properties } } Let SeaTunnel create every runtime file. data accepts YAML, properties and plain text; write each file as a triple-quoted value and mount it at the path the container reads. The example below replaces the engine configuration, both Hazelcast member configurations, logging, JVM options and the job file: kubernetes { job-config-file = job.conf configmap.runtime { name = seatunnel-runtime data.seatunnel.yaml = """ seatunnel: engine: classloader-cache-mode: true checkpoint: interval: 10000 timeout: 60000 """ data.hazelcast-master.yaml = """ hazelcast: cluster-name: seatunnel network: port: auto-increment: false port: 5801 """ data.hazelcast-worker.yaml = """ hazelcast: cluster-name: seatunnel network: port: auto-increment: true port: 5802 """ data.log4j2_client.properties = """ rootLogger.level = INFO rootLogger.appenderRef.console.ref = console appender.console.type = Console appender.console.name = console """ data.jvm_options = """ -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=2g """ data.job.conf = """ env { job.mode = "BATCH" parallelism = 2 } source { FakeSource { plugin_output = "example" row.num = 10 schema { fields { id = int } } } } sink { Console { plugin_input = "example" } } """ mount.seatunnel.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/seatunnel.yaml mount.hazelcast-master.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/hazelcast-master.yaml mount.hazelcast-worker.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/hazelcast-worker.yaml mount.log4j2_client.properties = /opt/seatunnel/config/log4j2_client.properties mount.jvm_options = /opt/seatunnel/config/jvm_options mount.job.conf = /opt/seatunnel/config/job.conf } master.hazelcast-config = hazelcast-master.yaml worker.hazelcast-config = hazelcast-worker.yaml } note Referenced ConfigMaps are never modified or deleted; their mounted keys are validated before submission. When the submitting identity cannot read a referenced ConfigMap, validation is skipped with a warning and the Pod still mounts it through its own service account. note Created ConfigMaps are named name or <application-id>-<entry>, carry the Job owner reference and disappear with the application. Set name when another option must reference the ConfigMap. tip Every key is mounted individually through subPath, so a ConfigMap never hides the other files the image ships in the same directory. Referenced keys and created keys may not share a mount path. Runtime file options pick the mounted paths: kubernetes.seatunnel-config-file (engine configuration), kubernetes.master.hazelcast-config / kubernetes.worker.hazelcast-config, kubernetes.jvm-options-file plus the role-specific files, kubernetes.log4j-config-file and kubernetes.job-config-file.

kubernetes.env.<NAME> injects one variable per name; the value is a literal, a Secret key reference secret:<name>/<key> or a ConfigMap key reference configmap:<name>/<key>. kubernetes.env-from.secret / kubernetes.env-from.configmap inject every key of an existing object at once: kubernetes { env { JOB_MODE = "BATCH" # literal value MYSQL_PASSWORD = "secret:platform-job-secrets/password" # secretKeyRef ENGINE_FILE = "configmap:platform-engine-config/seatunnel.yaml" # configMapKeyRef } env-from.secret = platform-extra-secrets } Injected values reach the master Pod environment, where ${VAR} placeholders in the job configuration - inline or mounted - are resolved. note An explicit env.<NAME> wins over a duplicate key from env-from, and Kubernetes skips envFrom keys that are not valid environment variable names.

Application mode passes the distribution JVM option files to the JVM through the Java @argfile syntax: the common jvm_options first, then jvm_master_options in the master container and jvm_worker_options in worker containers. Mount replacements through kubernetes.configmap and they take effect without any other change: kubernetes.configmap.jvm-options { ref = platform-jvm-options mount.jvm_master_options = /opt/seatunnel/config/jvm_master_options mount.jvm_worker_options = /opt/seatunnel/config/jvm_worker_options } Set kubernetes.master.jvm-options-file or kubernetes.worker.jvm-options-file to an absolute path for a different location, or to disabled to pass no argument file for that role. note The mandatory Java 11+ module flags (--add-opens / --add-exports) used by Hazelcast and the Kerberos configuration reload are always appended, so a mounted file only adds or overrides options. Logging uses kubernetes.log4j-config-file (default log4j2_client.properties, console appenders so kubectl logs stays readable). Set it to log4j2.properties to use the distribution's file-based server configuration, and mount that file at the configured path; logs then go to <seatunnel-home>/logs.

application { name = "example-batch" worker-count = 2 master.memory-mb = 1024 master.cpu-cores = 1 worker.memory-mb = 2048 worker.cpu-cores = 2 worker.slots = 4 startup-timeout-millis = 180000 } kubernetes { namespace = seatunnel image = "registry.example.com/seatunnel/application:3.1.0" image-pull-policy = IfNotPresent service-account = seatunnel-application job-config-file = job.conf # Platform-managed runtime files; job.conf is selected explicitly above. configmap.runtime { ref = platform-runtime-config mount.seatunnel.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/seatunnel.yaml mount.log4j2_client.properties = /opt/seatunnel/config/log4j2_client.properties mount.hazelcast-master.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/hazelcast-master.yaml mount.hazelcast-worker.yaml = /opt/seatunnel/config/hazelcast-worker.yaml mount.jvm_options = /opt/seatunnel/config/jvm_options mount.job.conf = /opt/seatunnel/config/job.conf } # Credentials stay in a Secret; the job references them with ${VAR}. secret-ref = platform-job-secrets env { MYSQL_PASSWORD = "secret:platform-job-secrets/password" } master.hazelcast-config = hazelcast-master.yaml worker.hazelcast-config = hazelcast-worker.yaml checkpoint-pvc = seatunnel-checkpoints finished-job-retention-seconds = 86400 } bin/seatunnel-application.sh submit --target kubernetes -a kubernetes.conf
caution Pod requests equal limits. Plan worker count, worker slots, job parallelism, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, and node capacity together. The master does not provide task slots.

Kubernetes Application Mode creates an independent Kubernetes application for one SeaTunnel job. A batch/v1 Job hosts the only Zeta master. The master requests a fixed number of worker Pods. Every process uses the same SeaTunnel image, and worker and application resources are cleaned up when the job terminates. Use it when Kubernetes manages compute resources and jobs require isolated resources, dependencies, and failure boundaries. Execution uses the native Zeta Engine without Flink or Spark.

Component Kubernetes resource Responsibility Application master One Job Pod Start the Zeta master, create workers, submit the job, and coordinate cleanup Worker N regular Pods Join the isolated Hazelcast cluster and provide fixed task slots Job configuration Inline master environment; optional mounted job.conf kubernetes.job-config-file selects a ConfigMap or Secret file; unset keeps the submitted -c file Runtime configuration Existing or created ConfigMap Mounted read-only by the master and workers with seatunnel.yaml, Hazelcast, JVM option and logging files Master discovery Master Pod IP Workers join the advertised Pod IP over TCP; the headless Service only selects the master Pod Checkpoint PVC or supported remote storage Preserve recoverable state outside the application caution Losing the master or any worker fails the current Job. Workers are not replaced and no standby master is started. A new application can restore from a durable checkpoint.

A failed application can be resumed from its last durable checkpoint with application.restore-job-id.

An existing namespace, ServiceAccount, and minimal RBAC. An existing ConfigMap with the SeaTunnel runtime configuration, or the kubernetes.configmap.<entry>.data route that has SeaTunnel create one. Application Mode runs one isolated Zeta cluster per job. The submitter creates a suspended Kubernetes Job plus its dependencies, starts it and returns immediately; the master Pod starts the fixed workers, runs exactly one job, releases the workers and exits.

The application image is the standard SeaTunnel distribution with the Kubernetes resource manager in resource-managers/kubernetes/. Use a released image that includes Application Mode, or build your own to pick up unreleased changes or extra connectors.
docker pull apache/seatunnel:<version> docker tag apache/seatunnel:<version> registry.example.com/seatunnel:application

Build the distribution from source: ./mvnw -Prelease,seatunnel -pl seatunnel-dist -am -DskipTests -Dskip.ui=true package Build the image from the produced archive: FROM eclipse-temurin:11-jdk ADD apache-seatunnel-<version>-bin.tar.gz /opt/ RUN mv /opt/apache-seatunnel-<version> /opt/seatunnel ENV SEATUNNEL_HOME=/opt/seatunnel WORKDIR /opt/seatunnel Put apache-seatunnel-<version>-bin.tar.gz from seatunnel-dist/target/ next to the Dockerfile (the ADD path is relative to the build context) and build the image: cp seatunnel-dist/target/apache-seatunnel-<version>-bin.tar.gz . docker build -t registry.example.com/seatunnel:application . Either way, kubernetes.image must name an image the cluster can pull: push it to a registry, or load it into a local cluster (minikube image load, kind load docker-image). note The image must contain starter/, config/, lib/, connectors/ and resource-managers/kubernetes/, plus every connector, format and driver used by the job.

apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: seatunnel-apps --- apiVersion: v1 kind: ServiceAccount metadata: name: seatunnel-application namespace: seatunnel-apps --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: seatunnel-application namespace: seatunnel-apps rules: - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["create", "list", "watch", "delete", "deletecollection"] - apiGroups: ["batch"] resources: ["jobs"] verbs: ["get"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: seatunnel-application namespace: seatunnel-apps subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: seatunnel-application namespace: seatunnel-apps roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: seatunnel-application --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: Role metadata: name: seatunnel-application-submitter namespace: seatunnel-apps rules: - apiGroups: ["batch"] resources: ["jobs"] verbs: ["create", "get", "patch", "delete"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["pods"] verbs: ["list", "deletecollection"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["services"] verbs: ["create", "delete"] - apiGroups: [""] resources: ["configmaps"] verbs: ["create", "delete"] --- apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind: RoleBinding metadata: name: seatunnel-application-submitter namespace: seatunnel-apps subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: seatunnel-submitter namespace: seatunnel-apps roleRef: apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind: Role name: seatunnel-application-submitter kubectl apply -f application-rbac.yaml Replace the submitter subject with the identity that runs bin/seatunnel-application.sh.

Start from config/v1.kubernetes.conf.template, which already carries a demo job, and set the platform options: cp config/v1.kubernetes.conf.template kubernetes.conf application { name = "example" worker-count = 2 } kubernetes { namespace = "seatunnel-apps" image = "registry.example.com/seatunnel:application" service-account = "seatunnel-application" # The demo job is mounted from a ConfigMap SeaTunnel creates for this application, so the first # submission needs no -c file. job-config-file = job.conf configmap.job-conf { data.job.conf = """ env { job.mode = "BATCH" parallelism = 2 } source { FakeSource { row.num = 10 split.num = 2 schema { fields { id = int, name = string } } } } sink { Console {} } """ mount.job.conf = "/opt/seatunnel/config/job.conf" } } note Every mounted key needs its full container path; two entries cannot share one path. The created ConfigMap is named <application-id>-job-conf and is deleted with the application. To keep the job in its own file instead, pass it with -c job.conf and remove job-config-file.

bin/seatunnel-application.sh submit --target kubernetes -a kubernetes.conf bin/seatunnel-application.sh status --target kubernetes --id APPLICATION_ID -a kubernetes.conf --wait bin/seatunnel-application.sh cancel --target kubernetes --id APPLICATION_ID -a kubernetes.conf kubectl -n seatunnel-apps get jobs,pods,services kubectl -n seatunnel-apps describe job APPLICATION_ID kubectl -n seatunnel-apps logs job/APPLICATION_ID note No -c file is needed because the deployment file carries the job. submit returns as soon as the API accepted the started Job, so slow image pulls or scheduling never fail the command. Use status --wait (or submit --wait) when you need the terminal result. See Commands for every argument, the exit-code contract, and the kubectl inspection patterns.
High-frequency questions about operations, lifecycle, failures and security for Application Mode. Commands live in Commands, full option tables in Configuration.

bin/seatunnel-application.sh status --target kubernetes \ --id ACTUAL_APPLICATION_ID --application-config kubernetes.conf bin/seatunnel-application.sh cancel --target kubernetes \ --id ACTUAL_APPLICATION_ID --application-config kubernetes.conf Cancellation deletes the Job and labeled Pods, Service, and any Secret or ConfigMap created for the application. It does not create a savepoint, and referenced Secrets or ConfigMaps are never modified. Status returns UNKNOWN after deletion or Job TTL expiry.
documents.s: How do I inspect or cancel an application?

documents.t: kubectl -n seatunnel-apps get jobs,pods,services,secrets \ -l seatunnel.apache.org/application-id=ACTUAL_APPLICATION_ID kubectl -n seatunnel-apps logs job/ACTUAL_APPLICATION_ID kubectl -n seatunnel-apps describe job ACTUAL_APPLICATION_ID Inspect every worker Pod when diagnosing worker failures. Image pull, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, admission, and node-capacity problems normally appear in Pod events.
documents.s: How do I inspect resources and logs?

documents.t: The master exit code produces a Job Complete or Failed condition. The completed master Pod, Service, and any created Secret or ConfigMap remain until kubernetes.finished-job-retention-seconds expires. If the master is forcibly terminated before cleanup, workers exit after losing the master, but stopped Pod objects may remain until Job TTL cleanup. Retry cancel after an API outage is resolved.
documents.s: How long are completed resources retained?

documents.t: The Job stays Active and status --wait keeps polling; --wait-timeout bounds that wait. For unattended batch runs, set kubernetes.active-deadline-seconds so Kubernetes fails the Job automatically and --wait returns FAILED. Fix the root cause from the Pod events: image pull, admission policy, ResourceQuota, or node capacity.
documents.s: What happens when the master Pod never starts?

documents.t: Symptom Check Master Pod never runs Image pull, admission policy, ResourceQuota, node capacity, and submitter kubeconfig permissions Workers do not register Service, NetworkPolicy, master port, ServiceAccount permissions, and worker events A file is missing in a Pod The referenced ConfigMap/Secret name and key, and the full mount path, must match; referenced keys are validated before submission. Connector not found Matching plugins and drivers under the image connectors/ directory Job failure has no obvious cause Master logs, every worker log, and kubectl describe job/pod Checkpoint recovery fails Historical Zeta job ID, PVC or remote storage access, retention policy, and configuration consistency

Use a dedicated namespace and least-privilege ServiceAccount. Mount the API token only in the master; workers do not require it. Manage private image credentials through the ServiceAccount or cluster. Restrict application Secret access and enable Kubernetes encryption at rest for Secrets when required by the cluster's security policy. Keep connector credentials out of logs and prefer credential mechanisms supported by the connector, filesystem, or cluster. Put kubernetes.kubeconfig in a permission-restricted deployment configuration file, or use the Kubernetes SDK default. Do not pass it with -i because command-line arguments may be visible to other users on the submission host. Allow only required Hazelcast and external-system traffic in NetworkPolicy.

Application Mode deploys one self-contained SeaTunnel application per submission: the resource platform starts a dedicated Zeta master and a fixed number of workers, the master runs exactly one job, and the platform reclaims every process when the application finishes. Zeta itself owns worker registration, slot scheduling, task execution and checkpoints; the resource platform only provides and reclaims compute. That boundary is what lets the same job run on different platforms without changing the job file.

A job runs once, its result is written, and every resource it held is released immediately: no long-running cluster to keep warm and no leftover processes to clean up by hand. The application state maps directly to platform objects, so status and cancel are enough to observe and stop it.

Teams that run many batch jobs at the same time get per-job isolation: every job owns its master and its fixed set of workers, with its own CPU, memory and slot footprint, namespace and labels. One job cannot borrow slots from another or disturb its state, and quotas and policies apply per application. Checkpoints survive the application, so a later application can restore an earlier job by its native job ID.

You already operate a resource platform and do not want to maintain a long-running shared SeaTunnel cluster. Every job should own an isolated cluster with a fixed resource footprint. The job lifecycle should be visible and manageable through platform objects.

Many small jobs should share one long-running cluster (use standalone or cluster deployment). The job needs dynamic worker scaling or automatic worker replenishment while it runs; Application Mode uses a fixed worker set and fails instead of scaling out. The distribution has no provider for your resource platform.
documents.s: When not to use Application Mode

documents.t: One application runs one Zeta master and a fixed number of workers; no member is added or removed while the job runs. Workers register their slots with the master before the job starts. The master maps the job result to the platform state and releases the workers before it exits. Checkpoints live in engine-owned persistent storage and survive the application; a new application can restore them by native job ID.

A supported resource platform provider must be present in the distribution. The platform must be able to start and observe the dedicated processes and clean them up when the application ends. Credentials stay outside the job file: inject them through platform-managed secrets and resolve them with ${VAR} placeholders inside the application. Platform-specific preparation, permissions and configuration are described in the platform guide.

Term Definition Application One job plus its dedicated master and fixed workers, identified by the platform-native ID. Master The single Zeta member that runs the job, coordinates workers and publishes the result. Worker A fixed-size Zeta member that registers slots and executes tasks. Resource manager The Engine component that owns worker lifecycle through a platform driver. Resource manager driver The platform provider implementation that starts, observes and releases worker processes. Application specification The immutable, platform-independent application fields carried to the master. Localized specification The platform mechanism that delivers the specification to the master, such as mounted files or injected environment variables. Checkpoint Engine-owned durable state in persistent storage; independent of the application lifecycle.
The command line reference documents submitting, inspecting, waiting for and cancelling an application; the platform guide covers the environment its provider needs.

SeaTunnel jobs are defined declaratively. Instead of writing code for most integrations, you describe the execution environment, the source side, optional transforms, and the sink side in a configuration file. This guide explains the structure of a SeaTunnel job, how data flows between plugins, and how to move from the built-in sample to a real pipeline.

Most SeaTunnel jobs follow the same top-level structure: env { parallelism = 1 job.mode = "BATCH" } source { FakeSource { plugin_output = "fake" row.num = 16 schema = { fields { name = "string" age = "int" } } } } transform { FieldMapper { plugin_input = "fake" plugin_output = "renamed" field_mapper = { name = user_name age = age } } } sink { Console { plugin_input = "renamed" } } At a high level: env controls how the job executes source defines where data comes from transform changes data in-flight sink defines where data goes

The env block contains execution-level settings. Some keys are common across engines, while others are engine-specific. Common settings usually include: Key Meaning job.mode BATCH or STREAMING parallelism Default parallelism for the job job.name Optional display name for the job checkpoint.interval Checkpoint interval for streaming jobs and exactly-once workflows If you use Flink or Spark, engine-specific settings are also configured in env. See JobEnvConfig for the detailed engine parameter rules.

The source block describes how SeaTunnel reads data from an external system. A source usually includes: connector name connection parameters read scope, such as table, topic, path, or query schema or format-related parameters plugin_output so downstream plugins can refer to this output explicitly If you use multiple sources in one job, naming each source output clearly will make the pipeline easier to read and maintain.

The transform block is optional. Use it when the data needs to be filtered, renamed, enriched, mapped, or validated before it reaches the sink. Typical use cases: rename or map fields filter rows convert row kinds run SQL transforms validate data before writing SeaTunnel supports going directly from source to sink. If no transform is needed, you can omit this block completely.

The sink block defines how SeaTunnel writes data to the target system. A sink usually includes: connector name connection parameters target table, topic, or path write semantics or batching parameters plugin_input pointing to the upstream source or transform output Different sinks expose different options. Use the relevant connector document for exact option names, defaults, and examples.

These two keys are the most important conventions for understanding how data moves through a SeaTunnel job. plugin_output names the data stream produced by a source or transform plugin_input tells a transform or sink which upstream stream to consume This is especially useful when: one job reads from multiple sources one transform fans out into multiple sinks different branches of a job should remain easy to understand If a job has only one upstream path, SeaTunnel can often follow the default convention without requiring both fields. Explicit naming is still recommended for readability.

SeaTunnel supports multiple configuration styles: HOCON: the default and most commonly used format JSON: useful when configuration is generated by another system SQL: useful when expressing jobs in SQL-oriented workflows Use these references for format-specific details: Config Concept SQL configuration

The fastest way to build a real job is to replace the sample plugins gradually: Keep the env block from the sample. Replace FakeSource with a real source connector. Replace Console with the target sink connector. Add transforms only when the source schema and target schema do not align directly. Add connector-specific jars or drivers if required. For example: MySQL to Doris Kafka to Iceberg S3File to StarRocks PostgreSQL CDC to Kafka
documents.s: Moving From The Sample To A Real Job

documents.t: Before running a job, verify these points: Java and JAVA_HOME are set correctly required connector plugins are installed third-party drivers are present if required source credentials and network access are valid target table, topic, or path already exists when required job.mode matches the connector capabilities you intend to use

Download​ docker pull apache/seatunnel:<version_tag> How to submit job in local mode # Run fake source to console sink docker run --rm -it apache/seatunnel:<version_tag> ./bin/seatunnel.sh -m local -c config/v2.batch.config.template # Run job with custom config file docker run --rm -it -v /<The-Config-Directory-To-Mount>/:/config apache/seatunnel:<version_tag> ./bin/seatunnel.sh -m local -c /config/fake_to_console.conf # Example # If you config file is in /tmp/job/fake_to_console.conf docker run --rm -it -v /tmp/job/:/config apache/seatunnel:<version_tag> ./bin/seatunnel.sh -m local -c /config/fake_to_console.conf # Set JVM options when running docker run --rm -it -v /tmp/job/:/config apache/seatunnel:<version_tag> ./bin/seatunnel.sh -DJvmOption="-Xms4G -Xmx4G" -m local -c /config/fake_to_console.conf Build Image By Yourself​ Build from source code. You can download the source code from the download page or clone the source code from the GitHub repository Build With One Command​ cd seatunnel # Use already sett maven profile sh ./mvnw -B clean install -Dmaven.test.skip=true -Dmaven.javadoc.skip=true -Dlicense.skipAddThirdParty=true -D"docker.build.skip"=false -D"docker.verify.skip"=false -D"docker.push.skip"=true -D"docker.tag"=3.1.0 -Dmaven.deploy.skip -D"skip.spotless"=true --no-snapshot-updates -Pdocker,seatunnel # Check the docker image docker images | grep apache/seatunnel Build Step By Step​ # Build binary package from source code sh ./mvnw clean package -DskipTests -Dskip.spotless=true # Build docker image cd seatunnel-dist docker build -f src/main/docker/Dockerfile --build-arg VERSION=3.1.0 -t apache/seatunnel:3.1.0 . # If you build from dev branch, you should add SNAPSHOT suffix to the version docker build -f src/main/docker/Dockerfile --build-arg VERSION=3.1.0-SNAPSHOT -t apache/seatunnel:3.1.0-SNAPSHOT . # Check the docker image docker images | grep apache/seatunnel The Dockerfile is like this: FROM eclipse-temurin:11-jdk ARG VERSION # Build from Source Code And Copy it into image COPY ./target/apache-seatunnel-${VERSION}-bin.tar.gz /opt/ # Download From Internet # Please Note this file only include fake/console connector, You'll need to download the other connectors manually # wget -P /opt https://dlcdn.apache.org/seatunnel/${VERSION}/apache-seatunnel-${VERSION}-bin.tar.gz RUN cd /opt && \ tar -zxvf apache-seatunnel-${VERSION}-bin.tar.gz && \ mv apache-seatunnel-${VERSION} seatunnel && \ rm apache-seatunnel-${VERSION}-bin.tar.gz && \ sed -i 's/#rootLogger.appenderRef.consoleStdout.ref/rootLogger.appenderRef.consoleStdout.ref/' seatunnel/config/log4j2.properties && \ sed -i 's/#rootLogger.appenderRef.consoleStderr.ref/rootLogger.appenderRef.consoleStderr.ref/' seatunnel/config/log4j2.properties && \ sed -i 's/rootLogger.appenderRef.file.ref/#rootLogger.appenderRef.file.ref/' seatunnel/config/log4j2.properties && \ cp seatunnel/config/hazelcast-master.yaml seatunnel/config/hazelcast-worker.yaml WORKDIR /opt/seatunnel

Mount Spark/Flink library​ By default, Spark home is /opt/spark, Flink home is /opt/flink. If you need run with spark/flink, you can mount the related library to /opt/spark or /opt/flink. docker run \ -v <SPARK_BINARY_PATH>:/opt/spark \ -v <FLINK_BINARY_PATH>:/opt/flink \ ... Or you can change the SPARK_HOME, FLINK_HOME environment variable in Dockerfile and re-build your and mount the spark/flink to related path. FROM apache/seatunnel ENV SPARK_HOME=<YOUR_CUSTOMIZATION_PATH> ... docker run \ -v <SPARK_BINARY_PATH>:<YOUR_CUSTOMIZATION_PATH> \ ...

The command is different for different engines and different versions of the same engine, please choose the correct command. Spark # spark2 docker run --rm -it apache/seatunnel bash ./bin/start-seatunnel-spark-2-connector-v2.sh -c config/v2.batch.config.template # spark3 docker run --rm -it apache/seatunnel bash ./bin/start-seatunnel-spark-3-connector-v2.sh -c config/v2.batch.config.template Flink before you submit job, you need start flink cluster first. # flink version between `1.12.x` and `1.14.x` docker run --rm -it apache/seatunnel bash -c '<YOUR_FLINK_HOME>/bin/start-cluster.sh && ./bin/start-seatunnel-flink-13-connector-v2.sh -c config/v2.streaming.conf.template' # flink version between `1.15.x` and `1.18.x` docker run --rm -it apache/seatunnel bash -c '<YOUR_FLINK_HOME>/bin/start-cluster.sh && ./bin/start-seatunnel-flink-15-connector-v2.sh -c config/v2.streaming.conf.template' # flink version `1.20.x` docker run --rm -it apache/seatunnel bash -c '<YOUR_FLINK_HOME>/bin/start-cluster.sh && ./bin/start-seatunnel-flink-20-connector-v2.sh -c config/v2.streaming.conf.template'

You can run docker logs -f seatunnel_master, docker logs -f seatunnel_worker_1 to check the node log. And when you call http://localhost:8080/system-monitoring-information, you will see there are 3 nodes (1 master and 2 workers) as we expected. After that, you can use client or restapi to submit job to this cluster.
